{{Short description|Polyhedron with seven sides}}
[[File:Chestahedron.png|thumb|upright|A [[Chestahedron]], realized with 4 equilateral-triangle and 3 [[Kite (geometry)|kite]] faces, all having the same area,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://frankchester.com/chestahedron-geometry/|title=The Geometry of the Chestahedron|author=Frank Chester|access-date=8 August 2022}}</ref>]]

A '''heptahedron''' ({{plural form}}: '''heptahedra''') is a [[polyhedron]] having seven sides, or [[face (geometry)|faces]].

A heptahedron can take a large number of different basic forms, or topologies. The most familiar are the [[hexagonal pyramid]] and the [[pentagonal prism]]. Also notable is the [[tetrahemihexahedron]], which can be seen as a tessellation of the [[real projective plane]]. No heptahedra are [[regular polyhedron|regular]].

==Topologically distinct heptahedron==
===Convex===
There are 34 topologically distinct ''convex'' heptahedra, excluding mirror images.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.numericana.com/data/polycount.htm|title=Counting polyhedra|date=5 April 2015|website=numericana.com }}</ref> (Two polyhedra are "topologically distinct" if they have intrinsically different arrangements of faces and vertices, such that it is impossible to distort one into the other simply by changing the lengths of edges or the angles between edges or faces.) 

An example of each type is depicted below, along with the number of sides on each of the faces. The images are ordered by descending number of six-sided faces (if any), followed by descending number of five-sided faces (if any), and so on.

===Concave===
{{More citations needed|section|date=February 2026}}
{| class=wikitable style="background:white; max-width: 32em;"
|- valign="top" 
| colspan="2" | <gallery mode="nolines" widths="110px" style="text-align: center;">
File:Heptahedron concave 03.svg
File:Heptahedron concave 04.svg
File:Heptahedron concave 05.svg

File:Heptahedron concave 07.svg
File:Heptahedron concave 08.svg
</gallery>
Six topologically distinct concave heptahedra (excluding mirror images) can be formed by combining two [[tetrahedra]] in various configurations. The third, fourth and fifth of these have a face with collinear adjacent edges, and the sixth has a face that is not [[simply connected]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Heptahedron |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Heptahedron.html |access-date=2025-12-04 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>
|- valign="top"
| [[File:Heptahedron concave 01.svg|110px|center]][[File:Heptahedron concave 02.svg|110px|center]]
13 topologically distinct heptahedra (excluding mirror images) can be formed by cutting notches out of the edges of a triangular prism or square pyramid. Two examples are shown.
| [[File:Heptahedron concave 09.svg|110px|center]][[File:Heptahedron concave 10.svg|110px|center]]
A variety of [[simply connected|non-simply-connected]] heptahedra are possible. Two examples are shown.<ref>https://www.researchgate.net/publication/296814860_Regularization_of_heptahedra_using_geometric_element_transformation_method</ref>
|}

[[File:Szilassi polyhedron.svg|thumb|right|The Szilassi polyhedron]]
One particularly interesting example is the [[Szilassi polyhedron]], a [[toroidal polyhedron]] with 7 non-convex six sided faces.<ref name=szilassi>{{citation
 |last    = Szilassi
 |first   = Lajos
 |journal = Structural Topology
 |pages   = 69–80
 |title   = Regular toroids
 |url     = http://www-iri.upc.es/people/ros/StructuralTopology/ST13/st13-06-a3-ocr.pdf
 |volume  = 13
 |year    = 1986
}}</ref>
